title: Bottling Up Your Emotions
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano argues that bottling up emotions does not make them disappear but instead becomes a channel for 'drift,' his term for behavior pulling away from what a person considers coherent. He opens with his own experience of being told as a boy not to cry, then uses the survival show Alone as a case study, noting that nearly a third of contestant exits are psychological and highlighting a contestant who realized in isolation that burying his feelings was working against him. The analytical core distinguishes expressive suppression from experiential avoidance and ties both to the perseverative cognition hypothesis and allostatic load, arguing that unprocessed emotions keep stress active long after the triggering event. He then sketches how that load feeds self-reinforcing stress loops that spill into sleep, work, and relationships. His remedy runs through his 'return loop' of noticing, regulating, choosing, and acting, with cognitive reappraisal offered as the practical alternative to avoidance and suppression. Although the piece opens with a masculinity angle, its operational target is personal emotional discipline for anyone, which keeps it in Leadership rather than Family.
points: Zambrano distinguishes expressive suppression (hiding outward signs) from experiential avoidance (refusing to feel at all), treating both as forms of bottling up.
The Alone example shows that isolation removes external demands and makes the internal world louder, so buried feelings return with more force.
Through the perseverative cognition hypothesis, he argues that rumination keeps a stressor physiologically active, building allostatic load over repeated unprocessed events.
Accumulated load feeds interlocking cycles, for example poor sleep that hurts work performance, which then adds new stress back into the emotional loop.
Cognitive reappraisal is presented as the constructive alternative: examining what a feeling means and how the situation is being interpreted, then acting on that judgment.
quotes: We are in a society that is teaching youth, especially boys, that being vulnerable is a weakness and that feeling emotions is a recipe for failure.
That’s what isolation does. Your environment becomes more predictable and stops demanding more attention, so your mind shifts its attention inward. Your internal world gets louder.

Basically, changing your behavior when emotions happen so you can hide them, at least on the outside. Bottling things up, though, is more than that. It includes experiential avoidance — plainly avoiding the experience or the feeling — as well.

Before I begin talking about this, though, I want to introduce an idea: the perseverative cognition hypothesis. This is a framework that, in a nutshell, states that a physical stressor doesn’t need to be there to keep causing stress.

The thing is that burying your feelings not only impacts you as an organism, but also how you interact with others, your identity, how you perceive yourself, and, consequently, your own behavior. Bottling things up is then a channel for drift.
Cognitive reappraisal does something fundamentally different from avoidance: it changes our interpretation of a situation in order to change how it impacts us.
Honestly, I think “letting go” after reappraising is also valid, as long as letting go stems from a real acceptance of the situation rather than avoidance.
Remember, brushing things off is okay, as long as you really deem them unimportant. Otherwise, reappraise.
